title: The Stone Halls
subtitle: A walking exhibit of cathedrals and castles

halls.title: The Round Arch
halls.blurb: Walls thick as a fortress, arches turned on a compass, windows kept small because the wall was still doing all the work. Europe stops building in wood and starts building for a thousand years.

halls.title: Lux Nova
halls.blurb: Three old tricks — the pointed arch, the rib vault, the buttress — are put together at once outside Paris, and the wall dissolves into coloured glass. An abbot calls the result a new light.
halls.epigraph: The dull mind rises to truth through material things.

halls.title: The Age of Cathedrals
halls.blurb: A century of competitive vertigo. Vaults climb from thirty-seven metres to forty-two, tracery is invented, and towns mortgage themselves to out-build the next valley over.
halls.epigraph: Higher, and thinner, and full of light.

halls.title: Stone and Siege
halls.blurb: The same masons, the same geometry, the opposite intention. Here architecture is designed to be shot at — and to make the person approaching it feel very small.
halls.epigraph: Every wall here has an angle of fire.

halls.title: Flame and Fan
halls.blurb: Structure has been solved, so the rib goes decorative: fans, nets, stars, stone that behaves like frost on a window. The cathedral becomes a cage of glass with a lace ceiling.
halls.epigraph: When the problem is solved, the pattern begins.

halls.title: Dome and Drama
halls.blurb: Antiquity is rediscovered and immediately exceeded. The pointed arch is put away; in its place a dome, a portico, a colonnade that reaches out and takes you by both arms.
halls.epigraph: I will build the Pantheon over the Temple of Peace.

halls.title: The Long Echo
halls.blurb: The Middle Ages are rebuilt on purpose — some out of scholarship, some out of longing, one out of pure geometry. Two of these buildings were finished more than six centuries after they were begun.
halls.epigraph: My client is not in a hurry.
